passages.t: ‘I am the LORD your God, who brought you out’
passages.happening: “And God spoke all these words: ‘I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery’” (verses 1-2). These are the first words God speaks from the mountain to all the people.
passages.hearers:
These are the only words in the book that God speaks directly to the whole people. Everything else in the law comes through Moses, at the people's own request (verse 19).

Notice how they begin. Not with a command, but with a name and a rescue. God says who he is, ‘the LORD your God’. Then he says what he has done: brought you out of slavery. Only after that does he say what Israel must do. Grace comes before command. That order governs everything that follows.

The Ten Commandments are given to people already set free. They are not a ladder Israel must climb to earn God's favor. They are the shape of life for a people who already belong to the God who rescued them.

Scholars have compared this opening with ancient treaties, in which a great king names himself, recalls what he has done for a people, and then lays down what they must do. The comparison shows that the commandments are the terms of a relationship with a king who has already acted.
passages.later:
Moses later reminds Israel that God spoke these words “to your whole assembly out of the fire, the cloud, and the deep darkness on the mountain; He added nothing more” (Deuteronomy 5:22).

Jesus did not set the commandments aside: “I have not come to abolish them, but to fulfill them” (Matthew 5:17).
passages.hard:
How are the Ten Commandments numbered? The Bible never numbers them. It calls them the ‘ten words’ (34:28), from which the Greek name Decalogue comes, and different traditions divide them differently.

Jewish tradition counts verse 2, ‘I am the LORD your God’, as the first word, and joins ‘no other gods’ and ‘no idols’ (verses 3-6) as the second.

Catholics and Lutherans, following Augustine, join ‘no other gods’ and ‘no idols’ as the first commandment, and divide the command against coveting (verse 17) into two, so that coveting a neighbor's wife and coveting his goods are the ninth and tenth.

The Orthodox and Reformed churches, following an older division found in the Jewish writers Philo and Josephus and in Origen, count ‘no other gods’ and ‘no idols’ as two separate commandments, the first and second.

The words are the same in every tradition; only the count differs. So when two Christians speak of the second commandment, they may be pointing to different verses. The traditions also divide the two tablets differently: Philo put five on each, Augustine three and seven, Calvin four and six.
passages.asks: God's first word is not ‘do this’ but ‘I brought you out’. Ask whether you obey God to earn his love, or because you already have it. And ask what slavery God has brought you out of, and how remembering it changes the way you hear his commands.

passages.t: No other gods, and no idols
passages.happening:
“You shall have no other gods before Me” (verse 3).

“You shall not make for yourself an idol in the form of anything in the heavens above, on the earth below, or in the waters beneath. You shall not bow down to them or worship them; for I, the LORD your God, am a jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers on their children to the third and fourth generations of those who hate Me, but showing loving devotion to a thousand generations of those who love Me and keep My commandments” (verses 4-6).
passages.hearers:
The first command does not argue that no other gods exist. It forbids Israel to treat any other power as a god. It asks for undivided loyalty, within a relationship God has already begun.

The second forbids making an image. The three zones, heavens, earth, waters, are the whole created world of Genesis 1. Nothing God made may be used to stand for him.

Every neighboring people made images of their gods, and an image was not just a picture. In Mesopotamia a ritual was performed to bring a god's presence into a new statue, which was then clothed, fed and carried in procession. Forbidding images meant that Israel's God could not be located, handled or managed. Deuteronomy gives the reason from Sinai itself: Israel heard a voice and saw no form.

Archaeology shows how hard this was. Many small clay figures have been found in houses in Judah from the 700s and 600s BC. The command was not obvious even inside Israel.

Christians have differed over what the image command means for worship. The Second Council of Nicaea in 787 approved honoring icons, on the ground that God became visible in Christ. The Reformed churches rejected images in worship. Both read the same command, and both agree that nothing made may be worshiped as God.

‘Jealous’ here is not insecurity or spite. Many interpreters, Jewish and Christian, point out that it describes a husband's rightful passion for his marriage. Indifference to a loved one's unfaithfulness would be a lesser love, not a greater one.
passages.later:
Moses later gives the reason for the image law: “You heard the sound of the words, but saw no form; there was only a voice” (Deuteronomy 4:12).

The New Testament says God has given his own image: “The Son is the image of the invisible God” (Colossians 1:15), and “No one has ever seen God, but the one and only Son, who is Himself God and is at the Father’s side, has made Him known” (John 1:18).

Ezekiel answers those who blamed their troubles on their parents: “The soul who sins is the one who will die. A son will not bear the iniquity of his father, and a father will not bear the iniquity of his son” (Ezekiel 18:20).
passages.hard:
What does ‘visiting the iniquity of the fathers on their children to the third and fourth generations’ mean? The verse can trouble readers, and it should be read carefully, beside the rest of the Bible.

The Bible itself raises the question. Deuteronomy 24:16 says “each is to die for his own sin”. Ezekiel forbids the old proverb about the fathers eating sour grapes and the children's teeth being set on edge, and says plainly, “A son will not bear the iniquity of his father” (Ezekiel 18:20).

Jewish interpreters faced this early. An old Aramaic translation reads verse 5 as applying to children who go on sinning as their fathers did, and the Talmud explains the two passages the same way. The verse's own words point there too: it speaks of ‘those who hate Me’. Others note that three or four generations was the span of one household living together in the ancient world. So the verse describes how one generation's idolatry damages everyone under its roof, a pattern still seen in families. Ezekiel was answering people who used the old saying to blame their ancestors instead of turning back to God.

And the verse is lopsided on purpose. Judgment reaches a few generations of those who hate God. Loving devotion reaches ‘a thousand generations’ of those who love him.

So this verse is never a curse on any family. It does not mean that God punishes a child for a parent's sin, or that anyone is doomed by where they come from. No one is bound by a parent's choices. Anyone, from any family, may turn to God and find his loving devotion.
passages.asks: God's love reaches a thousand generations. Ask what patterns from your family you have carried, for good or ill. And ask what it would mean for you to begin something new, in God's loving devotion, for those who come after you.

passages.happening:
“You shall not take the name of the LORD your God in vain, for the LORD will not leave anyone unpunished who takes His name in vain” (verse 7).

“Remember the Sabbath day by keeping it holy. Six days you shall labor and do all your work” (verses 8-9). On the seventh day no one is to work, sons and daughters, servants, animals and the foreigner too (verse 10).

“For in six days the LORD made the heavens and the earth and the sea and all that is in them, but on the seventh day He rested” (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
The command about God's name concerns more than careless words. Names were used in oaths, curses and magic. The Hebrew speaks of lifting up the name ‘for emptiness’: using God's name to back a false oath, to curse, or to bend him to your will. Israel's courts relied on oaths, so lying in God's name attacked both his honor and justice itself.

The Sabbath is not new here. Israel already received it with the manna (16:23-30). Now they are told to ‘remember’ it.

The list of who must rest is longer than for any other command: children, male and female servants, animals, the foreigner. That is because the Sabbath was the day most likely to be denied to those under someone else's authority. In a world where most people worked without pause, a law giving slaves a day off by God's command was startling.

Here the reason is creation: God worked six days and rested on the seventh. Deuteronomy gives another reason for the same command: ‘Remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt’. The Sabbath rests on God's work in creation and on his rescue from slavery.

Christians differ on how to keep the Sabbath today. The note on Exodus 16 sets out the main views, and these notes take no side.
passages.later:
Deuteronomy grounds the same command in the exodus: “Remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt, and that the LORD your God brought you out of there with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm” (Deuteronomy 5:15).

Jesus says, “The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath” (Mark 2:27). Hebrews speaks of the rest still ahead: “There remains, then, a Sabbath rest for the people of God” (Hebrews 4:9).
passages.asks: The Sabbath gave rest to those who could never take it for themselves. Ask whether your way of living gives rest to those who work for you or with you. And ask whether you have used God's name to back up what you wanted, rather than to honor him.

passages.t: Parents, life, marriage, property, truth and desire
passages.happening:
“Honor your father and mother, so that your days may be long in the land that the LORD your God is giving you” (verse 12).

“You shall not murder. You shall not commit adultery. You shall not steal. You shall not bear false witness against your neighbor” (verses 13-16).

“You shall not covet your neighbor’s house. You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife, or his manservant or maidservant, or his ox or donkey, or anything that belongs to your neighbor” (verse 17).
passages.hearers:
The commands now turn from God to the neighbor. The fifth stands at the hinge. It is the first command with a promise.

‘Honor’ comes from the Hebrew word for ‘heavy’: to give someone weight. For adults it meant caring for parents and respecting them in old age, not only obeying them as a child. That is how Jesus applies it in Mark 7.

Three of the next commands are only two words long in Hebrew. Together they protect the neighbor's life, marriage, property and good name.

‘Murder’ is the deliberate, unlawful taking of a life. Adultery in biblical law meant sexual relations with a woman married or promised to another man. The command against stealing has no object in Hebrew; the Talmud and Rashi read it as kidnapping, the stealing of a person, while most interpreters take it in its plain breadth. False witness belonged at the town gate, where cases were heard; a false witness could cost a man his life or his land.

The last command reaches past acts to desire, which no court can judge. It shows that God's law looks at the heart.
passages.later:
Jesus presses these commands to the heart: “You have heard that it was said, ‘Do not commit adultery.’ But I tell you that anyone who looks at a woman to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matthew 5:27-28).

Paul sums them up: “The commandments ‘Do not commit adultery,’ ‘Do not murder,’ ‘Do not steal,’ ‘Do not covet,’ and any other commandments, are summed up in this one decree: ‘Love your neighbor as yourself’” (Romans 13:9).

Ephesians applies the fifth to Christian homes: “‘Honor your father and mother’ (which is the first commandment with a promise)” (Ephesians 6:2).
passages.hard:
Does ‘Honor your father and mother’ mean you must obey or stay with a parent who harms you? No.

Honor is not the same as obedience in everything, and it is never a duty to stay in harm's way, for a child or for a grown son or daughter. Paul joins this commandment to the words ‘obey your parents in the Lord’ (Ephesians 6:1-2). No parent can command what God forbids. The note on that passage says what must be said here too:

These words must never be used against a child who is being harmed. No one may use ‘obey your parents’ to keep a child quiet about abuse, or to send a child back to someone who is hurting them.

Abuse of a child is a crime. It is to be reported to the police and the proper authorities, not handled quietly inside a church. If a child is in danger, or you know of a child being harmed, contact the police or your local child protection service now. If you were harmed as a child, what was done to you was wrong, and it was not your fault. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

For grown children, honoring a parent can mean care and respect in their old age, as Jesus said. It never means pretending that harm was not harm, or going back into danger. Honor and safety are not enemies.
passages.asks: The last command reaches past what we do to what we want. Ask which of these commands touches your heart most closely this week. And ask what it would mean to love your neighbor, not only to avoid harming them.

passages.happening:
“When all the people witnessed the thunder and lightning, the sounding of the ram’s horn, and the mountain enveloped in smoke, they trembled and stood at a distance” (verse 18).

“‘Speak to us yourself and we will listen,’ they said to Moses. ‘But do not let God speak to us, or we will die’” (verse 19).

“‘Do not be afraid,’ Moses replied. ‘For God has come to test you, so that the fear of Him may be before you, to keep you from sinning’” (verse 20). “And the people stood at a distance as Moses approached the thick darkness where God was” (verse 21).
passages.hearers:
The people have heard God's voice, and it is too much for them. They ask for someone to stand between them and God. This is where Moses' role as go-between for all the laws that follow begins.

Moses' answer sounds like a contradiction: do not be afraid, because God has come so that you will fear him. He is drawing a line between two kinds of fear. One is panic that drives people away from God. The other is reverence that keeps them from sin. The first Moses takes away. The second he wants them to keep.

Moses goes into ‘the thick darkness where God was’. God is present, and he is hidden. Later Christian writers, among them Gregory of Nyssa, read Moses' entry into the darkness as the soul moving toward a knowledge of God beyond sight.
passages.later:
Moses later remembers this request as the origin of a promise: “This is what you asked of the LORD your God at Horeb on the day of the assembly” (Deuteronomy 18:16), and God promised a prophet like Moses (Deuteronomy 18:18), which Peter applies to Jesus (Acts 3:22). Paul writes, “there is one God, and there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Timothy 2:5).

Solomon recalls this darkness at the temple's dedication: “The LORD has said that He would dwell in the thick cloud” (1 Kings 8:12).
passages.asks: Moses told the people not to be afraid, and also to fear God. Ask which kind of fear you have of God: the kind that drives you away, or the kind that keeps you close and careful. And ask what it means to you to have a mediator who brings you near.

passages.happening:
God tells Moses to say, “You have seen for yourselves that I have spoken to you from heaven. You are not to make any gods alongside Me; you are not to make for yourselves gods of silver or gold” (verses 22-23).

“You are to make for Me an altar of earth” (verse 24). “In every place where I cause My name to be remembered, I will come to you and bless you” (verse 24).

If they build an altar of stones, they must not shape the stones with tools (verse 25). “And you must not go up to My altar on steps, lest your nakedness be exposed on it” (verse 26).
passages.hearers:
Here begins the collection of laws that 24:7 calls the Book of the Covenant, which runs to the end of chapter 23. It opens, like the ten words, with God, idols and worship.

Instead of an image, a simple altar of earth or of uncut stones. Using a tool on the stones would defile it. Human craft is kept out of the place of sacrifice. The ban on steps protected the modesty of the one offering, in the long robes of the day.

‘In every place where I cause My name to be remembered.’ This law assumes more than one place of worship, and Israel's early history shows altars at several places. Deuteronomy 12 later limits sacrifice to the one place God would choose. Scholars differ on how the two laws relate: some see this one as older, others read them as fitting together, with this law governing worship before one place was chosen.

And the promise: ‘I will come to you and bless you’. Worship is not Israel's way of reaching up to God. It is the place where God comes down.
passages.later:
Joshua obeyed this law: he built “an altar of uncut stones on which no iron tool has been used” (Joshua 8:31).

Jesus later said that true worshipers will worship the Father “in spirit and in truth” (John 4:23).
passages.asks: God wanted a plain altar, with nothing of human pride in it. Ask whether anything in your worship is more about display than about God. And ask what it means that God promises to come to the place where his name is remembered.
